summary:
The Riau Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The country overview records the same provision as carrying up to one year's imprisonment when a complaint is lodged.

No province-specific divergence from the national framework was found in the Riau Islands: private same-sex conduct is not separately criminalised here, but it also attracts no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection. A 2020 raid case in Indonesia illustrates how enforcement varies locally, with those held released because no regional regulation existed.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Physical risk is rising nationally. An October 2025 presidential decree lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among non-military threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy. In July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several cities including West Java, with no prosecutions reported; civil society describes rapidly worsening conditions. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge in vigilante attacks directly to officials' public condemnations and to that decree.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Two provinces of Indonesia, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity alongside national morality provisions; Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Neither province is the Riau Islands, but both illustrate the enforcement environment a visitor transits through.

Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. Pew recorded 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality morally unacceptable in 2025 and 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023.
tangentialFactors:
The Riau Islands' position as a transit and border zone between Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia means a visitor may pass through several legal regimes in a single trip, each with its own posture toward trans people. Aceh's caning regime and South Sumatra's provincial provisions show that sub-national divergence exists elsewhere in Indonesia even though none was found here.

Public opinion data indicates broad social hostility: Pew recorded 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality morally unacceptable in 2025 and 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023. Combined with the October 2025 presidential decree and the July 2026 mob attacks, this suggests a climate in which a visibly trans visitor may face hostility from members of the public as well as from officials.

Indonesia's votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025 signal the absence of international protection machinery a visitor could appeal to.

outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory records no unit-specific findings for the Riau Islands itself; the assessment rests on the national framework plus the explicit statement that no province-specific divergence was found here. Whether any Riau Islands district bylaw addresses same-sex conduct or gender expression is unresolved and not sourced.

The two figures for the extra-marital sex provision differ between sources: the parent framework states up to two years' imprisonment, while the country overview and this inventory state up to one year when a complaint is lodged. Both are carried here without reconciliation.

Whether the July 2026 mob attacks or the 22 June 2025 Puncak villa raid had any counterpart in the Riau Islands is not sourced. The 2020 raid case is cited for the general enforcement pattern; the inventory does not identify its location.
